I have gathered substantial material. Here are the verse-by-verse notes, drawn from the sources I was able to access. (I was unable to retrieve dedicated Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, or modern-scholarly pages due to search limits; where those traditions are absent, I note it.)

---

## Genesis 29 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: *Jacob resumed his journey and came to the land of the people of the east.*

- The Hebrew literally reads "Jacob lifted up his feet" — a unique idiom in the OT. It suggests a new energy and purpose after his encounter with God at Bethel (Gen 28). John Calvin says it "commends the extraordinary strength of Jacob's faith" and that he "traveled on briskly and cheerfully." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Ligonier (Reformed) notes there is "a new spring in his step" following Bethel; his journey will be speedy because he has begun to grasp God's promises. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-and-rachel
- "The land of the people of the east" refers to Mesopotamia / Haran, about 450 miles from Beersheba (Pulpit Commentary). Bible.org notes it can also refer broadly to northern Arabian tribes between Bethel and Haran. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 2: *He looked and saw a well in the field…three flocks of sheep…a large stone covered the mouth of the well.*

- This well is not the one where Eliezer met Rebekah (Gen 24), which was for village maidens near the town. This is a well in the open field for flocks, covered with a large stone (Pulpit). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm
- The large stone served to prevent evaporation, keep the water clean, or prevent unauthorized use (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- The scene is a familiar Oriental one: flocks waiting around a covered well at the heat of the day (Pulpit, citing *Land and Book* and Robinson's travels).

### v. 3: *When all the flocks had been gathered…the shepherds would roll away the stone…*

- This was the customary practice: wait until all flocks were assembled, then together roll away the stone and water them collectively. Possible reasons: convenience, preventing dust in the well from too-frequent opening, or ensuring equal distribution of water (Pulpit/Kalisch, Murphy). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm

### v. 4: *"My brothers," Jacob asked…"where are you from?"*

- "My brethren" was a customary friendly salutation, not implying literal family relationship. Calvin notes the "great frankness of that age" in greeting strangers as brothers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 5: *"Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?"*

- "Son of Nahor" here means grandson; Bethuel was Laban's father and Nahor his grandfather (cf. Gen 24:24, 29). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Jacob spoke Hebrew, the shepherds Chaldean. The dialects were not greatly dissimilar at that time, so they could converse (Pulpit/Gosman). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm

### v. 6: *"Is he well?"…"Yes, and here comes his daughter Rachel with his sheep."*

- "Is he well?" = literally "Is there peace (*shalom*) to him?" — meaning not just bodily health but all manner of felicity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Rachel = "ewe" in Hebrew (Gesenius). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm

### v. 7: *"Look," said Jacob, "it is still broad daylight…Water the sheep and take them back to pasture."*

- Two interpretations of Jacob's motive: (a) He wanted the shepherds to leave so he could meet Rachel alone (Keil, Lange, Murphy); or (b) his words reflect a naturally prudent and industrious character that disliked laziness (Starke, Kalisch, Bush). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm
- Bible.org suggests Jacob, himself a shepherd, knew this was against good shepherding practice and wanted both to correct them and to show off his strength for Rachel. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 8: *"We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered…"*

- Not because of physical inability (Jacob alone could do it), but because of an agreed-upon custom to water all flocks collectively. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm

### v. 9: *Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.*

- That Rachel kept the sheep herself, though Laban had servants, shows the frugality and industry expected of daughters in that age. Calvin observes it was "deemed disgraceful to educate children in idleness, softness, and indulgence." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Ligonier (Reformed) notes this sets her apart as a woman of industry like her aunt Rebekah (Gen 24; Prov 31:13–19). — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-and-rachel

### v. 10: *Jacob…rolled the stone away…and watered his uncle's sheep.*

- The phrase "his mother's brother" is repeated three times in this verse to stress with "the greatest possible stress that Jacob had met with his own relations, with 'his bone and his flesh'" (Pulpit/Kalisch). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm
- Jacob disregarded the shepherds' custom (waiting for all flocks), acting boldly for his kinswoman. Ligonier says the same tenacity that got Jacob into trouble with Esau now serves him well. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-and-rachel

### v. 11: *Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.*

- Jacob first made himself useful (watered the sheep), then disclosed his identity, then kissed Rachel, then wept — overcome with joy at finding relatives after his long journey and at God's guidance (Ellicott, Pulpit). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/29.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-29.html
- Calvin comments that the "chaste and modest mode of living" of that age permitted greater liberty; today, "impurity and ungovernable lusts" make even looks suspect. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Bible.org adds that weeping openly shows the cultural propensity of Oriental men to display emotion more freely than Western counterparts. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 12: *He told Rachel that he was Rebekah's son…and she ran and told her father.*

- The narrator's parallels with Genesis 24 (Rebekah at the well, running home) are deliberate. Ligonier says these are not coincidences: "The same Lord who found a wife for Isaac has now found one for Jacob." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-and-rachel

### v. 13: *When Laban heard…he ran out to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him.*

- The rabbis say Laban ran because he expected Jacob would bring rich presents as Eliezer had done (Gen 24:10). Bible.org says it is not yet necessary to impugn Laban's motives, though he will later out-manipulate Jacob. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Calvin: Jacob had probably been instructed by Rebekah about signs and marks by which to prove his identity; Laban was "induced by indubitable tokens to acknowledge Jacob as his nephew." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 14: *"You are indeed my own flesh and blood." After Jacob had stayed with him a month…*

- "My bone and my flesh" is the language of family recognition, echoing Gen 2:23. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Calvin notes that Laban used the month to test Jacob's character; Jacob was not idle but "employed himself in honest labors, that he might not in idleness eat another's bread for nothing." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 15: *Laban said…"should you work for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be."*

- Calvin reads Laban's offer of wages two ways: either it would be unjust to defraud a relative, or he was unwilling to extract free service under cover of kinship. He takes the second as the true sense. Yet Laban's general principle of equity is soon abandoned when personal gain is at stake — an example of how "men seldom err in general principles" but when it comes to their own affairs, "perverse self-love blinds them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Enduring Word notes that Jacob, the son of great wealth, was now being treated as a hired servant — a humbling reversal. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

**No specific Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Catholic, or Orthodox sources found for this verse.**

### v. 16: *Now Laban had two daughters; the older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel.*

- Leah: etymology disputed — Akkadian "cow," Arabic "wild cow," or Hebrew "wearied" (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Rachel: "a ewe" — nomadic peoples often named children after animals. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 17: *Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful.*

- The Hebrew adjective for Leah's eyes is disputed. Options: "weak" (NASB, RSV), "delicate" (NKJV), "lovely" (NRSV, TEV), "dull" (REB), or "attractive" (Peshitta). Most English translations take the Arabic root meaning "weak/thin" in this context. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Enduring Word says some think Leah's eyes were bad and she couldn't see well; others think her eyes lacked the sparkle and life of Rachel's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Clarke notes: "The chief recommendation of Leah was her soft and beautiful eyes; but Rachel was beautiful in her shape, person, mien and gait and beautiful in her countenance" — though most commentators take the view of our English translations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html (editor's note)
- Calvin: Jacob's preference for Rachel's beauty may have been a fault — "a very culpable want of self-government, when any one chooses a wife only for the sake of her beauty, whereas excellence of disposition ought to be deemed of the first importance." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 18: *"I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."*

- Seven years was a very generous dowry, far above normal (Enduring Word, Bible.org). Jacob didn't want to risk a refusal. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Calvin calls Laban's acceptance of the deal "shameful barbarity" — selling his daughter by way of barter, "making her the subject of a kind of barter." He ought to have given a dowry, not extracted labor. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Grant's Commentary (Brethren) adds: "Rachel did not belong to Laban, and both Jacob and Laban were totally wrong in placing a mercenary value on a wife." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/genesis-29.html

### v. 19: *Laban replied, "Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me."*

- "Stay with me" is a Qal imperative in Hebrew — an idiomatic way of accepting Jacob's offer. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 20: *So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her.*

- Words that "breathe the purest tenderness" (Kalisch, cited in Whedon). "Love capable of shortening seven laborious years into a term of insignificant brevity." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/genesis-29.html
- Enduring Word highlights this as the principle that "true love waits" — Jacob was willing to wait seven years. He also connects it to the "True Love Waits" movement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Calvin notes Jacob's chastity: though living under the same roof for seven years, he "conducted himself with modesty, and abstained from all impropriety." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 21: *"Grant me my wife, for my time is complete, and I want to sleep with her."*

- Jacob's words are plain: he had waited seven years and now wanted to consummate the marriage. Laban, however, was in no hurry — showing his manipulative character (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 22: *So Laban invited all the men of that place and prepared a feast.*

- The feast (Hebrew *mishteh*, from the root "to drink") was a wedding banquet. Barnes notes the feast in the bride's father's house lasted seven days. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/genesis-29.html

### v. 23: *But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her.*

- How was Jacob fooled? Three theories listed by Bible.org: (1) it was dark; (2) the bride was veiled (cf. Gen 24:65); (3) Jacob was drunk — the word "feast" comes from a root meaning "to drink," implying a wild party. Bible.org thinks option 3 fits the social context best. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Enduring Word notes that according to ancient customs, the wife was veiled until alone with her husband; Laban could easily arrange darkness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Leah's complicity: she was under her father's authority, as was Rachel. Enduring Word cites Leupold: "She may have loved Jacob secretly. She may have considered this her one chance to get a husband." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

### v. 24: *Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maidservant.*

- The Nuzi Tablets (describing Hurrian culture of the 2nd millennium BC) show this was common practice: if the daughter proved barren, the servant could bear children on her behalf (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 25: *When morning came, there was Leah! "What have you done to me?"…"Why have you deceived me?"*

- The deceiver is now deceived. Jacob (who exchanged the younger for the older with Isaac) now has the older exchanged for the younger by Laban. A clear case of reaping what he sowed (Enduring Word). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Enduring Word: "When Jacob deceived his father and cheated his brother, God did not change His plan…Instead, God took Jacob to the school of difficult experience to discipline him. This shows that a believer's disobedience may not derail God's plan for their life, but it will greatly affect how they experience it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Calvin says Jacob "rightly expostulates" about the fraud. Laban's supposed reason (v.26) is merely a pretext; he should have warned Jacob in advance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

**No specific Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Catholic, or Orthodox sources found for this verse.**

### v. 26: *"It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older."*

- This was an excuse, not a legitimate justification. Laban had never mentioned this custom during seven years of negotiation. He used it as a cover for extracting another seven years of labor (Enduring Word, Calvin). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 27: *"Finish this week's celebration, and we will give you the younger one in return for another seven years of work."*

- The "bridal week" (seven days of wedding feasting) was common in that culture (cf. Judges 14:12, 17; Tobit 11:18). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Calvin thunders against Laban: "Laban now is become callous in wickedness, for he extorts other seven years… Yea, of his own accord, he obtrudes his daughter as an object of merchandise… He not only involves his nephew in polygamy, but pollutes both him and his own daughters by incestuous nuptials." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Calvin adds that the Lord through Malachi (Mal 2:14) pronounces divorce more tolerable than polygamy. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html

### v. 28: *And Jacob did just that. He finished the week's celebration, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.*

- Jacob accepted because he had no other option (Enduring Word). But Calvin argues Jacob sinned: "He might have dismissed Leah, because she had not been his lawful wife… But Jacob reluctantly retains her as his wife, from whom he was released and free, and thus doubles his fault by polygamy, and trebles it by an incestuous marriage." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Whedon (Methodist) disagrees with Calvin on the incest charge, noting: "This bigamy of Jacob must not be judged directly by the Mosaic law, which prohibits marriage with two sisters at the same time (Lev 18:18), or be set down as incest (Calvin), since there was no positive law on the point in existence then." Yet he also says "it is not to be justified" — it arose "from sinful infirmities" and became "a true school of affliction to Jacob." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/genesis-29.html

### v. 29: *Laban also gave his servant girl Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant.*

- Like Zilpah with Leah (v.24), this follows the Nuzi custom of providing a maid who could bear children for a barren wife (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

### v. 30: *Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years.*

- The favoritism is stated plainly and sets up the family dysfunction to follow. Enduring Word: "Not only had Jacob married two sisters, but he also allowed everyone to know that one was favored and loved more than the other." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Grant's Commentary (Brethren) offers a typological/spiritual reading: Rachel ("sheep") typifies the lovely state of soul in humble submission that believers desire, while Leah ("wearied") pictures what I really am — the struggle of Romans 7. "In struggling to get Rachel, he only got Leah." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/genesis-29.html

### v. 31: *When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren.*

- The Hebrew word here is literally "hated" (*sane*), but it is a Hebrew idiom of comparison meaning "loved less" (see Deut 21:15; Mal 1:2–3; cf. Luke 14:26). Bible.org: "It speaks of priority. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Clarke (Methodist) explains forcefully: "The word simply signifies a *less degree of love*… Jacob did not hate her in the sense in which this term is used among us; but he felt and showed less affection for her than for her sister." He warns against using this text to support certain theological "peculiarities of their creed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-29.html
- Calvin: "Moses here shows that Jacob's extravagant love was corrected by the Lord; as the affections of the faithful, when they become inordinate, are wont to be tamed by the rod." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Enduring Word: "God's compassion on Leah is touching. She was truly the innocent party in all this mess. God can bring comfort and blessing to a wife and meet her needs even when the husband acts in an ungodly manner." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Enduring Word cites Luther's vivid description: "Wretched Leah sits sadly in her tent with her maid and spends her time spinning and weeping…There the poor girl sits; no one pays any attention to her." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

### v. 32: *Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now."*

- Reuben = "Behold, a son" (from the Hebrew verb "to see"). The popular etymology connects it to "the LORD has looked on my affliction." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Calvin notes Leah was not ungrateful to God: she "not only acknowledges God as the author of her fruitfulness; but also assigns as a reason, that her affliction had been looked upon by the Lord." He adds it is probable she had been praying. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Enduring Word observes sadly: "Jacob, even though he did not love Leah, still was willing to have sex with her. This demonstrates a principle that is still true, that a man will often be willing to have sex completely apart from love, and only a foolish woman regards the willingness to have sex as proof of love." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

### v. 33: *Again she conceived…and she named him Simeon.*

- Simeon = "Hearing" (from Hebrew *shama*, "to hear"). Leah said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- The birth of Reuben had not turned Jacob's heart. Leah was still aware he did not love her (Enduring Word). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

### v. 34: *Once again Leah conceived…she named him Levi.*

- Levi = "Attachment/joined" (from Hebrew *lavah*, "to join"). Leah hoped: "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29
- Enduring Word: "The pain in the heart of Leah was just as evident as the hardness of Jacob's heart." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/

### v. 35: *And once more she conceived…"This time I will praise the LORD." So she named him Judah. Then Leah stopped having children.*

- Judah = "Praise" (from Hebrew *yadah*, "to praise"). For the first time, Leah does not mention her husband or her pain; she focuses on God alone. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- This marks a spiritual turning point. Enduring Word: "Leah stopped naming her children to reflect the pain and longing in her heart. At this point, she focused on God and could praise Him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/
- Calvin: "In her fourth son, she again declares her piety towards God, for she gives to him the name of 'praise,' as having been granted to her by the special kindness of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-29.html
- Barnes: "Well may she praise the Lord; for this is the ancestor of the promised seed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/genesis-29.html
- Enduring Word and Bible.org both emphasize that the Messiah came through Leah, not Rachel. The two greatest tribes — Levi (priestly) and Judah (royal) — came from the "less-attractive sister who was neglected and despised but learned to look to the Lord and praise Him." This reversal of expected outcomes shows God's sovereignty. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-29/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-29

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

| Issue | Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier) | Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke, Whedon) | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jacob's polygamy | Calvin calls it sin — incestuous and polluting. Jacob could have dismissed Leah lawfully. | Whedon disagrees on "incest" charge since no Mosaic law yet existed, but agrees it was not justified and came from "sinful infirmities." | Emphasizes the messiness as God's discipline; Jacob reaped what he sowed. Polygamy not explicitly condemned here but seen as tragic. |
| "Leah was hated" (v.31) | Calvin: "hated" means not loved enough; God corrected Jacob's inordinate love. | Clarke: vigorously argues "hated" = "less loved." Warns against misusing the text for Calvinistic doctrines of reprobation. | Guzik: "unloved" — God's compassion for Leah is the emotional heart of the chapter. |
| Providence theme | God's "secret providence" (Calvin) and "hidden providence" (Ligonier) govern all — the well meeting is no coincidence. | Not specifically different in available sources. | God's unseen hand is emphasized, but more through narrative parallels than doctrinal language. |

**Traditions not found in searches**: Baptist (Spurgeon, Desiring God/John Piper, GTY), Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org), Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes). These could not be retrieved due to search limits.
